newsitem.title: ITALY: FORECAST-Italy rate cut no aid to lower BTP yields.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Italy rate cut no aid to lower BTP yields.

text.p: Italian bond yields are expected to creep up over the coming quarter even if the Bank of Italy can see its way to lowering official interest rates, economists polled by Reuters said.

Current political uncertainty and concern that European economic and monetary union (EMU) may not start on time make bond yields over the next three months hard to predict, as shown in a quarterly Reuter survey of analysts' forecasts.

Economists' expectations for the benchmark 10-year fixed rate government bond (BTP) yield at the end of June vary by two points, with the average 7.85 percent -- a little above the current yield of 7.63 percent on Wednesday.

The spread over the 10-year German bund is seen wider at 194 basis points compared to 177 today. This is not taking into account a possible cut in Italy's discount rate which most economists see falling to 6.00-6.25 percent from 6.75 currently.
One of the most pessimistic forecasts came from brokers Caboto which sees the yield on the 10-year BTP at 8.40 percent by the end of June and the discount rate unchanged.
Caboto economist Giovanna Mossetti said the forecast was based on "the risk surrounding the euro and the risk of yield rises in Europe in reaction to the rise in U.S. T-bond yields".
This is seen within a picture of increasing economic activity in Europe, Mossetti said.
But if German unemployment falls, as Caboto expects, there will not be pressure from Germany for a delay in EMU and Italy would gain from such a scenario.
"Even if Italy has to enter in a second wave, the pressure to reduce the deficit in a structural way will remain," and markets would reward Italy with a rise in BTPs, she said.
Analysts on average expect 10-year BTP yields at the end of this year to be around 7.82 percent, little changed from June, with the spread seen at 177 basis points.

One brokerage, which declined to be named, saw market expectations for an official rate cut causing market rates to fall. This would allow the Bank of Italy to keep a strict stance and not cut official rates, before tightening policy in 1998.
Several economists expected official rates to rise in 1998 due to an upturn in the European economic cycle which could push up German rates, causing other Europeans to follow.

But Credito Italiano economist Lorenzo Stanca saw room for Italian easing still this year, with two official rate cuts between now and the end of the summer due to falling inflation, which is unlikely to rise in the second half of the year, and due to lira steadiness.
Analysts said a discount rate cut did not increase the room for a fall in bond yields between now and June, with BTPs likely to suffer as the debate on the future of EMU rumbles on.
But towards the end of the year the market was likely to recover on the expectations of a favourable solution to Italy's controversial bid to join EMU at its start, Stanca said.
On that basis, Credito saw 10-year BTPs yielding 7.0 percent by the year end with a sharp fall in the BTP spread over Bunds.
Investment house JP Morgan saw a narrow window between April and early May for an official rate cut due to falling inflation and improved EMU prospects as Germany's economy started to recover.

After that the situation was likely to become more complex with possible tensions over Italy's 1998 budget and an expected increase in U.S. interest rates, which would leave BTP yields holding around the levels they are today.
